Title: The Thirty-Six Hours
Author: Mae Lindqvist
Image Alt: A leather holdall resting on a hotel bed
Excerpt: Thirty-six hours in another city. What goes in the bag — and what stays behind.
Body HTML:
I have been refining this list for about four years. Before that, I packed the way most people pack: with good intentions and a complete failure of nerve. Three pairs of shoes for a weekend. The coat I love but never wear. The dress I bought for an occasion that has never quite arrived.

Now I carry a single holdall. It weighs about six kilograms when full. Inside: two pairs of trousers, one jacket, three tops, one dress that does evening without trying, a pair of flat leather mules, a cashmere half-zip, and underwear. That is all. That is always all.

The Four Rules

The rules came slowly, through failure. Rule one: every piece must touch two other pieces. A trouser that only works with one top is not a trouser — it is a hostage situation. Rule two: nothing that needs ironing. Creases are fine. Ironing boards in hotel rooms are not. Rule three: colour lives in accessories, not in clothes. Rule four: bring one thing that is purely for pleasure — a silk scarf, a small perfume, a book with a good spine.

The Brera Trouser is in every bag I take. It has been to Lisbon, to a friend's house in the Lot, to three press days in Paris, and once, memorably, to a conference in Helsinki in February where I underestimated the weather. It survived all of it.

The test of a wardrobe is not how it looks in a photograph. It is how it holds up on the second day, when you are tired, when the weather has changed, and when you need to be somewhere new in forty minutes.

The other essential is the field coat. It is the piece I almost did not make — a coat that does not quite commit to being a coat, that works over everything and under nothing, that has two proper pockets and a lining you can feel is right. It has made every trip better. That is the only metric that matters.

Thirty-six hours is enough time to see whether a wardrobe actually works. It is too short to recover from a bad choice. I have not made a bad choice in about three years. I intend to keep it that way.

Title: On Wool, and Why We Never Use It Twice
Author: Elsa Mäkinen
Image Alt: Close detail of wool fabric texture
Excerpt: We use our wool exactly once. Here is what that means, and why it matters more than we initially thought.
Body HTML:
The wool comes from a small mill in the Biella region of northern Italy. We have been working with them for three seasons. They do not take new clients easily — you write a letter, you visit in person, you wait. We waited eight months. It was worth it.

What we mean when we say we never use a fabric twice is this: each season we select yarns and weights that are new to our range. Nothing is reordered. When a fabric is gone, it is gone. The garments made from it become, in a small way, unrepeatable.

Why It Matters

The fashion industry's relationship with textile surplus is complicated and mostly unexamined. Mills produce sample lengths. Brands order safety stock. Seasons turn and excess fabric is liquidated, destroyed, or simply stored in a warehouse somewhere in the Veneto, slowly yellowing.

We do not want to contribute to that. Every length of fabric we commission is cut to zero — meaning the full quantity becomes garments, and the garments are made in quantities small enough that we are confident they will all find homes.

Scarcity is not a marketing strategy. It is an acknowledgement that making things has consequences, and that those consequences deserve to be taken seriously.

The wool we are using this season is a 220-gram double-faced crepe from Loro Piana's reserve range. It has a handle unlike anything we have worked with before — firm enough to hold a line, light enough to drape. It makes exactly one garment in our collection: the Riva Coat. We made forty of them. When they are gone, this particular cloth will not appear again.

There is something clarifying about working this way. It forces us to ask, before we begin: is this fabric good enough to justify the time, the labour, the resources? If the answer is not an immediate yes, we do not proceed. Most things do not pass that test. A few do. Those are the ones we make.

Title: Fifty-Two Days: Inside the Porto Atelier
Author: Mae Lindqvist
Image Alt: Hands cutting fabric at a pattern-cutting table in an atelier
Excerpt: From first cut to finished garment: what actually happens in those fifty-two days.
Body HTML:
The number that surprises people most is not the price. It is the time. Fifty-two days, on average, from the moment the fabric is cut to the moment the finished garment is pressed, tagged, and folded into its box.

I spent three days in Porto last November watching this happen. Not in a self-congratulatory, brand-video way — I went because I needed to understand something I had been getting wrong, and I needed to see it with my own eyes.

Day One: The Cut

The atelier is on the second floor of a building near the river. The light in the morning is remarkable — flat and white, coming in from the north. Paulo, the pattern cutter who has worked here for twenty-three years, lays the fabric by hand. No automated cutting. Every piece is inspected before it is marked. A small imperfection in the weave — barely visible, something a machine would miss — is set aside. We do not cut around problems. We do not use that length.

This is the first of many moments where I think: this is what the price is for. Not luxury, not positioning. Time spent on judgment calls that most of the industry has automated away.

The Eleven Pairs of Hands

Between cutting and pressing, eleven people touch each garment. I wrote their names down: Paulo (cutting), Ana (first stitching), two seamstresses I did not catch the names of (seams and pressing the seams open), a specialist for the invisible zip, someone in their eighties whose title I did not understand but who checked every inside seam by feel, the quality inspector, the second press, the button attachment (done separately, by hand), the final check, and the woman who folds and boxes each piece with a deliberateness I found quietly moving.

At one point I asked how they knew when a garment was finished. Ana looked at me the way you look at someone who has asked a genuinely strange question. 'When it is right,' she said. I did not ask what right meant. I already knew.

What I got wrong, before I visited, was that I thought slow production was about values. It is about values, yes, but it is also about results. The garments that come out of this building hold their shape differently. The seams lie flat in a way that only happens when someone has pressed them open with care. The buttons sit correctly — a small thing that is, in fact, not a small thing at all.

I came back from Porto with a clearer sense of what we are making and why it costs what it costs. I also came back with a coat I bought from Paulo's wife at the market near the atelier on my last morning, made in a Portuguese cotton I had not seen before. I wear it constantly. It is not one of ours.

Title: The Discipline of One Colour
Author: Mae Lindqvist
Image Alt: Wide-leg linen trousers in bone laid flat on a stone surface
Excerpt: On the strange freedom that comes from choosing one palette and staying inside it.
Body HTML:
For three years I wore almost nothing that was not some shade of stone, bone, or chalk. People thought it was an aesthetic choice — a photographer's eye, an editor's discipline. It was neither. It was exhaustion. I was tired of deciding.

What happened, without my planning it, was that everything became easier. Getting dressed in the morning stopped being a series of negotiations. Things worked with other things. I stopped buying things impulsively because they were interesting and started buying things only if they were right.

The Palette Problem

Most people's wardrobes are not collections of clothes. They are accumulations of moods. A red dress purchased in a very specific state of mind that has not recurred. Trousers bought because a friend looked good in them. A coat in a colour that seemed brave in the shop and reads as mistake in real life.

The palette approach is not about neutrals — that is a misunderstanding. It is about deciding, once, what relationship you want to have with colour. My relationship is this: colour in small doses, in accessories, in single statement pieces. The rest is a foundation. The foundation does not change because foundations are not supposed to change.

There is a sentence I think about often, from a Japanese designer who made clothes for thirty years in the same grey. He said: restraint is not the same as refusal. He was right. I built a company on the difference.

What This Looks Like in Practice

My working wardrobe has eleven pieces. I have counted. The Brera Trouser in bone and in a dark charcoal. The field coat. Two cashmere knits in off-white. A silk camisole. A blazer in a wool-linen mix that goes with everything. Three shirts. A dress for evenings that asks nothing of me.

I add one piece per season, if I need to. I remove one for everything I add. This is not minimalism as performance. It is logistics as design philosophy. It works.

Title: How to Dress for a Morning That Will Last All Day
Author: Sofía Reyes
Image Alt: Woman in tailored trousers and a loose ivory shirt walking in morning light
Excerpt: A practical guide to the one outfit that carries you through a twelve-hour day without a change of clothes.
Body HTML:
The brief was this: a morning meeting, a lunch that runs long, an afternoon desk-sitting, an unexpected drinks that becomes dinner. One outfit. No bag-of-changes. The brief is not unusual. It is most days.

There are clothes built for occasions, and there are clothes built for time. The distinction matters more than anyone in fashion will admit. Occasion dressing is architecture — impressive, specific, inflexible. Time dressing is furniture. It accommodates. It persists.

The Components

The trouser is the foundation. A proper wide-leg — not fashion-wide, not costume-wide, but wide in the proportion that has worked for fifty years and will work for another fifty. The waist sits at the natural waist. The hem breaks gently over the shoe. When you sit, it still looks correct. When you stand, it looks more correct.

The top wants to be simple. A fitted knit, or a loose silk, or something in between. It does not need to be interesting. The trouser is the interesting piece. The top is the quiet part of a conversation.

The jacket is optional. But if you carry one — over the arm, not on the back — the evening becomes available. Without it, you are committed to wherever you are. The jacket is permission to be somewhere else.

On Shoes

Flat. Always flat. The heel, for a day this long, is a negotiation you will lose by three in the afternoon. A good leather mule, or a very clean trainer if the context allows, or a low-heeled loafer. The shoe should be something you can walk fast in, stand in for an hour, and still feel good about when you sit down to dinner.

The rest is maintenance: a small bag, a scarf that doubles as a wrap in cold rooms, and something that smells like you have made an effort even when you have not had time to make one. That is all. That is, in truth, everything.

Title: Why We Made Fewer Pieces This Season
Author: Mae Lindqvist
Image Alt: A single garment hanging on a simple wooden rail against a white wall
Excerpt: Resort 26 has twelve pieces. We considered eighteen. Here is why twelve was right.
Body HTML:
We started Resort 26 with a list of eighteen garments. At the final edit, six of them were removed. Some were good pieces — technically well-made, commercially logical, appropriate for the collection. We removed them anyway.

The question we ask at the end of every edit is: does this piece earn its place? Not 'is it sellable?' Not 'does it round out the range?' But: does this piece justify its own existence?

Two of the six failed because they were redundant — we had already solved that customer problem better elsewhere in the collection. Two failed because they were not quite right, and we did not have the time to make them right before the season, and we would rather not make them than make them badly. Two failed because they were ideas we liked in theory but that made no sense in the context of a twelve-piece wardrobe — the customer who buys this collection does not need this piece, even if she might want it.

The Case for Fewer

There is a perverse logic in fashion that says more means more confidence. A bigger collection is read as a stronger brand. We disagree. A bigger collection is a set of decisions made less carefully, spread thinner, representing a less articulate point of view.

Twelve pieces forces a clarity that eighteen would not. Every piece must relate to every other piece. The colour palette must work in every combination. The range of occasions covered must be genuine and coherent. With eighteen you can fudge it. With twelve you cannot.

What Was Cut

We will not say precisely — not out of secrecy but because naming absent things gives them weight they do not deserve. What we will say is that one of the cuts was a dress we had sampled three times and still could not get right. It is the dress I most wanted to make this season. We will try again for the next one.

The other cuts, we are at peace with. The twelve that remain are the twelve that should exist. That is the work.

Title: The Woman Who Wore the Same Coat for Seven Years
Author: Elsa Mäkinen
Image Alt: A woman in a long camel coat walking down a quiet cobblestone street in autumn
Excerpt: A portrait of the kind of woman we design for — and what she has taught us.
Body HTML:
She is an architect. She lives in Copenhagen, near the water. She has worn the same camel coat since the winter of 2018, and she plans to wear it for at least another seven years.

Her name is Ingrid. She showed me the coat on our third meeting — I had noticed it before but had not asked. The collar is slightly rolled now in a way it was not designed to roll. The buttons are the original ones. There is a repair on the right cuff that is so well done you have to be looking for it to see it.

'I bought it because it was right,' she told me. 'Not because it was fashionable or because I needed a coat. I needed a coat the way you need something that will work for ten years. That is a different need.'

What She Taught Us

Ingrid is the woman we design for. Not because she is our target demographic — although she is — but because she represents a relationship with clothes that we believe is both increasingly rare and increasingly right. She does not buy things because they are beautiful, though she notices beauty. She buys things because they are correct. The coat was correct. It still is.

We asked her what she would say to someone standing in a shop, trying to decide whether a coat was worth the price. She thought for a moment. 'Ask yourself if you can imagine still wearing it in ten years. Not if you will want to — if you can imagine it. If you can imagine it, buy it.'

The field coat we make exists because of conversations like this one. We wanted to make a coat that could be Ingrid's coat — that could be worn for seven years and then repaired and then worn for seven more. We do not know if we have succeeded yet. Ask us in 2033.

Title: What the Light Does to Linen
Author: Sofía Reyes
Image Alt: Linen fabric in natural bone colour catching afternoon light near a window
Excerpt: On the material that photographs like no other, and why we keep coming back to it.
Body HTML:
There is a moment, around four in the afternoon in a south-facing room, when linen does something no other fabric does. It catches the light and holds it. Not reflects — holds. The quality of the light changes as you move through the room, and the linen moves with it.

This is not poetic licence. Anyone who has photographed linen knows what I am describing. Our photographer, who spent three days shooting Resort 26, sent me a message on the second afternoon: 'I don't know what it is about this fabric.' I know what it is. It is the weave. It is the way the fibres are not perfectly even, the way the cloth breathes in a way that synthetic fibres cannot, the way age improves it rather than degrading it.

Why We Use Italian Linen

Linen is grown in many places. The best of it — the most consistently even, the most finely spun — comes from a region of northern Italy where the mills have been working with the same flax sources for generations. We use a 180-gram dress-weight linen that is also heavier than it looks, that drapes rather than falls, that holds its line without stiffness.

The Brera Trouser is made in it. The camisole is made in it. The dresses are made in it. They will all crease. That is correct behaviour. A linen that does not crease has been treated in a way that solves a problem by creating a worse one.

The crease is not a flaw. It is evidence of the fabric being alive — responding to movement, to body heat, to the specific shape of the person wearing it. After half an hour of wearing, linen belongs to you in a way cotton never quite does.

On Care

We recommend a cool hand wash, a gentle press if you want it, and the acceptance that the first wash will soften the hand slightly, and subsequent washes will soften it further, until the fabric reaches a state that cannot be replicated by anything other than wearing it. That state is the point. The journey from new to worn-in is the correct life of a linen garment.

Buy it. Wear it. Wash it. Wait. It will be worth the patience.
